creator: Jacob Rees-Mogg
title: The King could be a Muslim but not a Catholic
full_text:
Imagine you have become Prime Minister.
What would your priority be?
You have kissed hands. You've received
the seals of office. You've been clapped
into Downing Street South. You've
established Downing Street North. Your
writ runs through Whitehall and through
Westminster. You have a majority of 170.
You are the boss.
What do you want to do for your country
now? What is the burning issue that you
face?
Is it defense of the realm? Is it the
small boats and stopping illegal
migration? Is it the impending financial
crisis?
Well, if you're Andy Burnham, it's none
of these. It's an obscure piece of
legislation dating from 1829
on Catholic emancipation,
which he views as discriminatory.
And we know how with the left, D
I is almost as important
a religion as Christianity.
What does this act say? Well, its main
purpose was to prevent um the to remove,
rather, the disabilities that afflicted
Catholics
However, there was a concern that
Catholics were a bit dodgy,
a bit dangerous, and that they might
weasel their way into office, appoint
Anglicans to posts who were sympathetic
to Catholicism, and thereby pervert the
Anglican Church and take it over. So,
for this reason, it should not be lawful
for any person professing the Roman
Catholic religion directly or indirectly
to advise His Majesty
to make any appointments. And it goes
through a whole list of people other
than His Majesty and deputies touching
on or concerning the appointment to or
disposal of any office in the United
Church of England and Ireland or in the
Church of Scotland.
Anyone who did so, who was convicted by
due course of law, would be deemed
guilty of high misdemeanor
and disabled forever from holding any
office, civil or military, under the
crown.
>> [snorts]
>> Quite understandably,
Catholics were not allowed to make
appointments in the Anglican Church. In
another act, nor are Jewish people
allowed to do so. But Muslims and
Buddhists and Zoroastrians are.
Similarly, in the Act of Succession, the
king is allowed to be a Muslim or a
Zoroastrian, but not a Catholic. This is
the question that arises in terms of how
we have established our constitution.
Now, first of all, I think Andy
Burnham's proposal is ridiculous.
Speaking as a Catholic, I have no wish
to appoint bishops in the Church of
England. It's none of my business. It is
not the business of Catholics to make
appointments in other churches.
We don't recognize, under an encyclical
of Pope Leo the 13th, the validity of
Anglican orders. Why on earth should a
Catholic want to appoint to orders he
does not consider to be valid? Doesn't
make any sense. I can't imagine a Jewish
person would wish to appoint to orders
in the Anglican Church, either.
And likewise, the Anglican Church ought
not to have to suffer
from the appointment to its highest
offices being made by people who are not
of its faith, but of another faith.
Now, if the law is wrong,
it should be tightened so that only
Anglicans make this appointment. And if
the Prime Minister is not an Anglican,
something that didn't occur to them
would be a problem in 1829,
at that point, the most senior minister
who is an Anglican ought to advise the
king.
>> [snorts]
>> It doesn't really matter anymore because
the Anglican Church only gives one name
to the Prime Minister, so the Prime
Minister has become a rubber stamp. I
happen to think that's a mistake.
Nonetheless, the rubber stamp could be
applied by an Anglican minister before
getting on to the King for formal
appointment.
That seems to me to be a sensible
system. It could be done without any
change in legislation. It could be done
by practice rather than by law.
But if you wanted to change the law, the
law should be changed to stop
non-Anglicans making appointments rather
than the other way around.
However, once you start fiddling with
the Constitution,
you raise the issue of whether the
Constitution is itself fair.
I made this point when the succession
rights were changed so that women could
succeed equally with men.
If you're making one change, then you
are in a way updating, modernizing the
discrimination. You are bringing it to
today's date, whereas previously it had
been an historic anomaly. That it was
only men and that it was not Catholics
was an historic anomaly. If you change
one,
the discrimination on the other side
becomes more apparent, more deliberate,
more modern.
And therefore, if the Prime Minister
wanted to change this utterly trivial
debarring of Catholics from making
Anglican appointments, he should look at
the bigger discrimination.
Because if you look at the Act of
Settlement,
you see that everyone who inherits the
Crown must take various Protestant oaths
on becoming sovereign.
So, needs to be a Protestant on
succession.
But thereafter,
they can convert to any religion
that he wants.
So, the King, if he wants, could become
a Muslim.
He could become, if he wanted, a
Buddhist or a Hindu or a Zoroastrian. He
could be a Methodist. He could be a
Baptist. He could be a Seventh-day
Adventist. Whatever he wanted as long as
he's not a Catholic
as the law says um
the king must not be reconciled to or
hold communion with the C or Church of
Rome nor profess the Popish religion
or shall marry a Papist.
It's no longer the last bit.
But if the other bits are done, if he is
in communion with Rome or holds to the
Popish religion
then he is incapable of being king.
It is a discrimination exclusively
against Catholics. And I have no
objection to that
in the broad sweep of our island's
story.
I know and have studied the history of
the 17th and early 18th century. I know
why these acts were passed, what people
were worried about, the concerns about
the powers of the Papal See as a
temporal prince, of the hostility of
France
of the civil war that we had been
through
and of the incapacity of James II. I
understand why these laws were passed
and when they were historical anomalies,
they seemed to me to be perfectly
reasonable.
Now
we are updating our constitution but
leaving
this one extraordinary piece of
discrimination.
And in this instance, I would not
tighten the laws. I would not say that
the king cannot hold another religion if
he doesn't if he wishes to. Think it's
very unlikely that the king would wish
to hold a non-Christian religion, but I
wouldn't tighten the laws to make the
discrimination wider.
I would remove the bar on Catholics.
That would leave the anomaly
that the head of the Church of England
could be a Catholic.
But currently the head of the Church of
England could be a Muslim
and that doesn't seem to bother anybody
too much.
So, you could either just live with it
as it is and accept that the anomaly is
already there, and the only restriction
on the anomaly is a papistical one
against people like me who profess the
papish religion, which I'm very happy to
call it, by the way. I like being called
a papist. I am a papist.
I greatly admire the Holy Father.
Um
you could just leave it and say, "Well,
it's not going to be a problem, or if it
becomes a problem, we'll deal with it
then."
Or that the process of appointments is
now so bureaucratic, the king's role is
very limited, and the reality of being
head of the church is essentially a
title rather than a reality. The
Defender of the Faith, of course, a
Catholic title given to Henry VIII by
the then Pope.
Or there is a neater solution, which is
that the Regency Act should be used. So,
the most senior member of the royal
family who is in communion with the
Anglican Church should make
appointments. This may be a thing worth
doing anyway, because it's much more
likely that we have an atheist king or
an agnostic king
than we have a king who suddenly becomes
a Muslim or a Catholic.
So, I would change it as the laws are
being changed around discrimination.
As I say, it's a sleeping dog I would
have let lie.
And Burnham has decided to kick the dog.
Therefore,
the whole system needs to be sorted out,
not just a growling dog left having been
kicked.
As always, thank you very much for
watching.
Apologies for slightly mixed metaphor at
the end, but I think you got what I
meant.

notes.note: The monarch is Supreme Governor of the Church of England and must be a Protestant in communion with that Church. The Act of Settlement limits the Crown to Protestant heirs who join in communion, so a practising Muslim could not hold the role.
notes.claim: Currently the head of the Church of England could be a Muslim.
notes.context_quote: But currently the head of the Church of England could be a Muslim
notes.context_paragraph: That would leave the anomaly that the head of the Church of England could be a Catholic. But currently the head of the Church of England could be a Muslim and that doesn't seem to bother anybody too much.

sources.quote: The **Supreme Governor of the Church of England** is the [titular head](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titular_head "Titular head") of the [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England"), a position which is vested in the [British monarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_monarch "British monarch").
sources.explanation: Shows the monarch holds the Supreme Governor title, supporting the note's first claim.

sources.quote: Since the [Act of Settlement 1701](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Act_of_Settlement_1701 "Act of Settlement 1701"), all Supreme Governors have been members of the Church of England.
sources.explanation: Shows historic link between the role and Church of England membership after the Act of Settlement.

sources.quote: The Princess Sophia, Electress and Duchess Dowager of Hanover, Daughter of the late Queen of Bohemia, Daughter of King James the First, to inherit after the King and the Princess Anne, in Default of Issue of the said Princess and His Majesty, respectively and the Heirs of her Body, being Protestants.
sources.explanation: Shows the Crown is limited to Protestant heirs, supporting the Protestant-requirement claim.

sources.quote: That whosoever shall hereafter come to the Possession of this Crown shall joyn in Communion with the Church of England as by Law established
sources.explanation: Shows whoever takes the Crown must join in communion with the Church of England, supporting the communion requirement and the inference a practising Muslim could not hold it.
